issues.quote: a good end that in fact already fails puts the breaking commit outside the range; ... while an end that in fact already fails puts the breaking commit outside the search.
issues.text: The round-1 wording was pasted in without removing the clause it replaced, so the same consequence (an end that already fails puts the breaking commit outside the range/search) is stated twice in one sentence. Not wrong, but the repetition reads as two different conditions.

issues.text: I re-read this twice. "The listing" can be the code block or the output block, and the two commands are never written down, so I cannot line them up against the by-hand steps in the next sentence. What they do is stated, and the sentence after tells me exactly what the `...` hides, so I was not stuck — but I scrolled back three times to check I had not missed a line of the excerpt.
issues.fix: Say which listing: replace "The listing stops two commands before the end of the script" with "The excerpt above stops two commands before the end of the script".
issues.quote: The listing stops two commands before the end of the script. Those two commands drive the session to its end and close it

issues.text: "the next one" reads as the next commit in history, and that would mean a commit passing after one that failed — the opposite of the assumption section 4 told me the search rests on. I stopped, then guessed it means the next commit Git stopped on, which must be an older one.
issues.fix: Write "and printed `ok` at the next commit Git stopped on, an older one".
issues.quote: the check failed at the commit Git had already stopped on, and printed `ok` at the next one

issues.text: The output block shows `b3472f64d738ebe52e4441e8d15ca273d88d439a`, the prose shows `b3472f6`, and Expected result shows `b3472f6…`. Nothing says that a short prefix names the same commit, so I compared the two strings character by character before deciding they were the same one.
issues.fix: Add the bridge inside the sentence: "Git names `b3472f6` — the first characters of the long id in the listing — and prints it".

issues.text: I counted on my fingers and got three. Between the commit four back and the commit I am standing on there are three commits; the fourth is the one I am standing on, which is an end, not "in between". I read the sentence twice before deciding the count includes the newest commit.
issues.fix: Replace "one of the four commits in between" with "one of the four commits made since then".
issues.quote: So one of the four commits in between turned the first answer into the second, and two of them touch `total.sh`.

issues.text: This arrives with no instruction attached. I do not know what "experimental" costs me, and the sentence says `git checkout` does the same without telling me which one to type. At the one moment the lesson asks me to work by hand, I still do not know which command that is.
issues.fix: Close the sentence with the decision: "…and `git checkout` makes the same two moves, so either command works here."
issues.quote: Git 2.46's own manual labels `git switch` experimental, and `git checkout` makes the same two moves.

issues.text: Here `log₂` is used as if it were a thing you can have the same of. Section 4 gave me "the number of steps is the number of halvings — about log₂ of the commits between the ends", which I followed; "the same log₂ either way" made me stop and translate it back into that sentence.
issues.fix: Replace "because the work is the same log₂ either way" with "because the number of halvings is the same either way".
issues.quote: The less you know, the more it saves, because the work is the same log₂ either way.

issues.text: Option a is the Core concepts definition of the first bad commit with the id dropped in ("the oldest commit where the check fails; every commit before it passes"). I ticked it from memory of that bullet without thinking about the session at all, so it tests whether I read the list, not whether I understood the search.
issues.fix: Reword option a so the definition has to be applied, e.g. "If I check out the commit just before `b3472f6` and run `./test.sh` there, it prints `ok`."
issues.quote: Every commit before `b3472f6` in the searched range passes the check, since `b3472f6` is the oldest one where it fails.

issues.text: There is no such lesson for me to have read, so I came in without it and could not check what it was supposed to have taught me. Nothing here actually needed it — `HEAD`, checking out, and what a diff is are all glossed in this lesson — but I followed the link first and came back empty-handed.
issues.fix: Either order this lesson after that one exists, or add to the same line that everything this lesson borrows from it is glossed here.
